The verdict came down at 4:17 p.m. Guilty on all counts. The courtroom exhaled. The defendant showed no emotion. His lawyer shook her head. Outside, a crowd had gathered. Some cheered. Others wept. The case had divided the city for eighteen months. It began with a simple traffic stop. It ended with a trial that exposed deep fractures in the police department. The prosecutor presented forty-seven witnesses. The defense presented three. The jury deliberated for nine hours. Afterward, the foreperson said it was the hardest thing she had ever done. The victim's family issued a one-sentence statement. They said justice was overdue. The mayor called for reforms. He had called for reforms before. Nothing changed then. The question now is whether this verdict will be a turning point or just another moment that fades. History suggests the latter. The city deserves the former.
